newsitem.title: UK: Bunker collapse creditors to recover little-lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Bunker collapse creditors to recover little-lawyer.

text.p: A maritime lawyer said on Thursday that creditors of the Australian and New Zealand companies that collapsed as a result of a huge bunker trading scam stood to recover very little of their losses.
"Creditors are unlikely to recover more than a small dividend from the liquidation of SPET and Scollay," Ince & Co partner Jonathan Lux said,
Australian bunker trader SPET (South Pacific Energy Trading) went into liquidation in February 1996 followed by the collapse of New Zealand trader William Scollay & Co Ltd in March of the same year.
Speaking at a Bunker News European Convention in London, SPET liquidator Mark Chapple, a senior insolvency specialist with Baker & McKenzie, said SPET had amassed deficits of around $16 million.
SPET and Scollay had co-operated since 1992 when SPET was set up by Australian bunker trader Martin Lawson.
Lux said a number of shipowners have been called upon to pay twice for bunkers as a result of the collapse as various traders and suppliers had not received payments.
"Having paid once they are holding out not to pay twice and cases for their defence will go forward," Lux said.
SPET traded by drawing on credit lines supplied by Scollay to allow it to buy bunker fuels and supply them at a $4 to $5 discount per metric tonne, Chapple said.
It claimed to cover the losses on these transactions by investing payments it held for 30 days, before the bunkers' delivery, in derivatives.
Chapple said Scollay's New Zealand liquidators had been given dates in October to make a public examination of Lawson. Lawson has already been publicly questioned by Chapple.

SPET and Scollay drafted various bunkering services agreements during 1994 and 1995 by which SPET guaranteed not to hold more than $2.5 million on trust for Scollay and to ensure that Scollay was able to confirm all contracts entered into, Chapple said.

By January 1996, Scollay complained to SPET that it had not received nomination confirmations for at least 56 vessels and that SPET owed it about $3 million, plus another $3.2 million to an Australian subsidiary of Scollay.
Chapple said that Lawson had failed to trade derivatives in a major way and that it would have been difficult for him to use such trades to cover his bunker losses.

Lawson had come to rely on increasing bunker trading volumes to cover the next month's business, he said, and the resulting pyramid business collapsed when other traders started to lose confidence in SPET.
Chapple said: "It is my opinion that Lawson followed a strategy that was not sound for a sensible businessman. I have not seen evidence that millions of dollars have been salted away."
The Australian and New Zealand liquidators have agreed a protocol for the collection of debts and have placed funds recovered into a trust account until an ultimate decision can be made on payments.
